# Mechanical philosophy (explain by matter and motion, not hidden purposes) (`mechanical_philosophy`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by atomism, mechanical_clock, blood_circulation
- Core idea: Explain a natural process the way one explains a clock or a mill: by the shapes, arrangement and motions of its parts pushing on each other, and ask 'how does it work' before 'what is it for'. An explanation by a named power (opium causes sleep because it has a 'dormitive virtue') only restates the question. The approach is convincing where a model can be built: the heart as a pump with valves, the eye as a dark chamber with a lens, the limbs as levers. It is a research programme, not the last word: gravity, magnetism and later fields act without pushing parts, and living things need chemistry and evolution as well as mechanics.
- Pitfalls:
  - Concluding that animals are unfeeling machines, which historically excused cruel vivisection
  - Equating mechanism with godlessness; Boyle, Descartes and Newton saw the world-machine as evidence of its maker
  - Ridiculing purposes altogether; asking what an organ is for remains fruitful in anatomy (Harvey reasoned from the purpose of the vein valves)
  - Insisting everything works by contact; Newton's gravity was attacked by mechanists as an 'occult quality' and was right anyway
- History: greece: c. 430 BC – atomists explain all change by particles colliding; 3rd c. BC–1st c. AD Alexandrian mechanics and automata (Ctesibius, Hero); china: 1094 – Su Song's water-driven astronomical clock tower; cosmology stays organic rather than mechanical; islamic: c. 850 Banu Musa and 1206 al-Jazari build elaborate automata, without a mechanical philosophy of nature; europe: 1377 – Oresme compares the heavens to a clock; 1605 Kepler: the celestial machine is like clockwork; 1628 Harvey's heart as pump; 1644 Descartes, Principia philosophiae; 1660s Boyle names the 'mechanical philosophy'
- Read:
  - René Descartes, Principia philosophiae (1644)
  - Robert Boyle, The Origine of Formes and Qualities (1666)
  - E. J. Dijksterhuis, The Mechanization of the World Picture (1961)
